questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.problem: Find the first four non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\frac{1}{x+2}$ about the point $x=-1.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ and $a=e.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\ f(e) & =e\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)=e \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1 \\ {f}^{′}(e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(e) & =\frac{1}{e} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(e) & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =e+(2)(x-e)+\frac{(\frac{1}{e})}{2!}(x-e)^{2}-\frac{(\frac{1}{{e}^{2}})}{3!}(x-e)^{3}⋯ \\  & =e+2(x-e)+\frac{1}{2e}(x-e)^{2}⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x \\ f(1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}+1 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =1+1=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{‴}(1) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x & =1+2(x-1)+\frac{-1}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{2}{3!}(x-1)^{3}⋯ \\  & =1+2(x-1)-\frac{1}{2}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(x-1)^{3}⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $a=1.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} \\ f(1) & ={1}^{1/2}=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =1+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{(-1/4)}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)-\frac{1}{8}(x-1)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1.2$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{1.2}.$ Since

$$
1.2-1=\frac{1}{5},
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1.2} & ≈1+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{5})-\frac{1}{8}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{200} \\  & =\frac{219}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)$ about $x=0$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=0.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) \\ f(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{0+1}=1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(0) & =-\frac{1}{(0+1)^{2}}=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}} \\ {f}^{‴}(0) & =\frac{2}{(0+1)^{3}}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =(0)+(1)(x-0)+\frac{(-1)}{2!}(x-0)^{2}+\frac{(2)}{3!}(x-0)^{3}+⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=0.5$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.5).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡1.5 & ≈(0.5)-\frac{1}{2}(0.5)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(0.5)^{3} \\  & =0.417\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =1+(2)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{(4)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}) & ≈1+2(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =1+2(-\frac{\pi }{20})+2{(-\frac{\pi }{20})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{10}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{200} \\  & =0.735\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

questions.problem: Use the first three terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{10}.$ Give your answer to $5$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/2} \\ f(9) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =\frac{1}{6} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(9) & =-\frac{1}{108}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{108})(x-9)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)-\frac{1}{216}(x-9)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=10$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{10}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10} & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(10-9)-\frac{1}{216}(10-9)^{2} \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{216} \\  & =3.162\,04,\end{aligned}
$$

to five decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem: Use the first three terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x) = \sqrt x$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{9.1}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)	= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2 +\cdots,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/2} \\ f(9) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =\frac{1}{6} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(9) & =-\frac{1}{108}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{108})(x-9)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)-\frac{1}{216}(x-9)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x = 9.1$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{9.1}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9.1} & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(9.1-9)-\frac{1}{216}(9.1-9)^{2} \\  & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(0.1)-\frac{1}{216}(0.1)^{2} \\  & =3.016\,620,\end{aligned}
$$

to six decimal places. 

**Note:** The exact value of $\sqrt{9.1}$ is $3.016\,621$ to six decimal places. So, our approximation is very good!
